title.en: Why fund data needs a standard

description.en: Why the fund industry needs a common data format: how fund data travels between asset managers, administrators, custodians, distributors, insurers, data vendors and regulators; what goes wrong without a standard; how regulation drives the need for structured data; and how FundsXML, an open standard made by the fund industry, answers it.

say.en: Why does fund data need a standard? In this film you see how fund data travels, what goes wrong without a common format, and how FundsXML answers that. No knowledge of XML is needed.

en.title: Fund data travels a long way

say.en: Behind every investment fund, data travels a long way. The asset manager, the fund administrator and the custodian bank produce it. Distributors and fund platforms, data vendors, insurance companies and regulators need it: prices and net asset values, portfolios, costs, and a growing number of regulatory templates. Every one of these parties exchanges data with many others.

items.head: Valuation
items.text: The administrator calculates NAV and positions.

items.head: Asset manager
items.text: Checks the figures and adds fund data.

items.head: Distribution
items.text: Prices, costs and ESG data go to platforms.

items.head: Insurers
items.text: Receive the portfolio look-through.

items.head: Vendors & regulators
items.text: Get master data, prices and reports.

say.en: Take a single fund at month-end. The fund administrator calculates the net asset value and the positions. The asset manager checks the figures and adds its own fund data. Prices, costs and ESG data then go to fund platforms and distributors. Insurance companies that hold the fund need the full portfolio look-through. And data vendors and regulators receive master data, prices and reports. One fund, one date, and the same data travels to five places or more.

items.head: Every pair of partners agrees on its own files
items.text: Field names, codes and layouts differ from one interface to the next.

items.head: A new partner means a new interface
items.text: Mapping, testing and maintenance start again from scratch.

items.head: Every new rule is built many times
items.text: When regulation changes, each interface has to follow on its own.

items.head: Errors surface late
items.text: Often only at the receiver, when the data is already in use.

say.en: Without a common format, every pair of partners agrees on its own files, with their own field names and codes. A new partner means a new interface, with mapping and testing from scratch. When regulation changes, every one of these interfaces has to be changed on its own. And errors surface late, often only at the receiver, when the data is already in use.

en.title: What goes wrong without a standard

items.head: Which identifier?
items.text: One partner sends an ISIN, the next a WKN, the third its own internal number.

items.head: Same word, other meaning
items.text: Is 'price' the NAV, the issue price or the redemption price? Gross or net?

items.head: Versions drift
items.text: Each partner changes its format on its own schedule.

items.head: Manual fixes
items.text: Spreadsheets and e-mails fill the gaps, and errors slip through.

say.en: What goes wrong in practice? First, identifiers. One partner identifies a fund by its ISIN, the next one by a national code, and the third by its own internal number. Second, meaning. The same word can mean different things: is a price the net asset value, the issue price, or the redemption price, and is a cost figure gross or net? Third, versions drift. Each partner changes its format on its own schedule, and every change breaks someone else's import. And finally, manual work. Spreadsheets and e-mails fill the gaps, people re-type numbers, and errors slip through, often unnoticed until a client or a supervisor asks.

items.head: Interfaces
items.text: Each partner relationship needs its own mapping, tests and maintenance.

items.head: Manual work
items.text: Data is re-typed, re-formatted and checked by hand.

items.head: Errors
items.text: Wrong prices or holdings reach investors, insurers and regulators.

items.head: Time
items.text: Every new requirement takes months, because it is built many times.

say.en: These costs add up. Each partner relationship needs its own mapping, its own tests and its own maintenance. Data is re-typed and re-formatted by hand, and checked by hand. Errors reach investors, insurers and regulators, and every correction costs trust. And every new requirement takes months, because it has to be built many times over.

items.head: MiFID II
items.text: Distributors need costs and target markets for every fund.

items.head: PRIIPs
items.text: Key information documents need risk, cost and performance data.

items.head: SFDR
items.text: Sustainability data travels from fund to distributor.

items.head: Solvency II
items.text: Insurers look through to the holdings of every fund.

say.en: Over the last decade, regulation has become the main driver. MiFID II asks distributors to know the costs and the target market of every fund they sell. PRIIPs needs risk, cost and performance data for key information documents. The SFDR sends sustainability data from the fund to the distributor. And Solvency II asks insurers to look through to the real holdings of every fund. All of this is structured data, it changes regularly, and it has to arrive on time.

en.headline: The templates say what. FundsXML says how.
en.sub: FinDatEx defines the regulatory templates. FundsXML carries them, together with all other fund data, in one delivery.

say.en: For these needs, the industry body FinDatEx defines templates: which fields must be exchanged, and what they mean. But a template alone does not say how the data travels between systems. That is where FundsXML comes in: it carries these templates, together with all other fund data, in one delivery.

FundsXML is the answer: one common language for fund data. Instead of many bilateral formats, every party writes and reads the same format. A sender produces a file once, and every receiver understands it, in the same way.

items.head: Without a standard
items.text: Ten partners who all exchange data need up to forty-five interfaces.

items.head: With FundsXML
items.text: Each partner builds one: to read and write the common format.

items.head: New partner, same format
items.text: Joining a new partner becomes a matter of configuration, not a project.

say.en: The arithmetic is simple. Ten partners who all exchange data with each other need up to forty five bilateral interfaces. With a common format, each partner builds one: to read and write FundsXML. And a new partner no longer means a new project, because it speaks the same format.

items.head: Open and free
items.text: The schema and its documentation are published openly, free of charge.

items.head: Made by the fund industry
items.text: Started in 2001 by fund houses, not imposed by a regulator.

items.head: Run by an association
items.text: A not-for-profit association with open membership and working groups.

items.head: Built on XML
items.text: Every system can read it, every file can be checked automatically.

say.en: So what is FundsXML? It is open and free: the schema and its documentation are published, and anyone can use them without a licence fee. It was made by the fund industry itself. It started in two thousand and one, when fund houses looked for a common format for the data they exchanged every day. It is run by a not-for-profit association with open membership, and decisions are prepared in working groups by the people who use the standard. And it is built on XML, so every system can read it, and every file can be checked automatically.

en.title: From a German start to a European standard

items.text: Fund houses start a common format.
Version 1.0, under the German fund association BVI.

items.head: 2006 to 2013
items.text: Austria, the Netherlands, France, Denmark and Luxembourg join.

items.head: Today
items.text: Version 4, with the European regulatory templates.

say.en: In short, its history. It began in two thousand and one, with a group of fund houses. In two thousand and three, version one was published under the German fund association, BVI. Over the following years, Austria, the Netherlands, France, Denmark and Luxembourg joined. Today, version four carries the European regulatory templates, and the standard keeps growing with every new requirement.

items.head: ISO 20022
items.text: Messages for payments, securities and fund orders.

items.head: openfunds
items.text: A dictionary of fund attributes, often exchanged in tables.

items.head: FinDatEx
items.text: The regulatory templates and their fields.

items.head: FundsXML
items.text: Complete fund deliveries: master data, prices, portfolios, regulatory data.

say.en: Where does FundsXML fit among other standards? ISO 20022 covers messages, for example for fund orders and settlement. openfunds is a dictionary of fund attributes, often exchanged as tables. FinDatEx defines the regulatory templates. FundsXML brings it together in complete fund deliveries: master data, prices, portfolios, transactions and regulatory data, in one structured file. These standards work alongside each other; they do not compete.

items.head: Senders
items.text: Produce one format for all their partners, instead of one per partner.

items.head: Receivers
items.text: Load data from every fund house the same way.

items.head: Everyone
items.text: Automatic checks before the data moves on.

items.head: Lower cost of change
items.text: A new regulatory requirement is built into the standard once.

say.en: What does each party gain? Senders produce one format for all their partners, instead of one per partner. Receivers load data from every fund house the same way. Everyone can check a file automatically, before the data moves on. And when regulation changes, the new requirement is built into the standard once, and not into every single interface. In short: less effort for everyone, and data that can be trusted.

en.headline: One file, many receivers.
en.sub: The same delivery serves the distributor, the insurer and the data vendor. Each one takes the part it needs.

say.en: This is the key idea: one file, many receivers. The same delivery can serve the distributor, the insurer and the data vendor. Each one takes the part it needs, and nobody has to build a special file for each partner.
That was why fund data needs a standard. In the next film, you see what a FundsXML delivery contains. Thanks for watching.
